what_it_does: Self-driving cars and robots use 3D sensors (called LiDAR) that produce millions of individual distance measurements per second, known as a point cloud. Detecting objects such as cars and pedestrians in these point clouds is computationally expensive because every frame contains an enormous number of points that must be processed. DAWN observes that much of the scene stays the same from one frame to the next — most points are background — and exploits this redundancy. It partitions each new frame into regions around previously detected objects and compares those regions to the previous frame using a 3D similarity measure; points that are sufficiently similar to the last frame are filtered out as redundant and skipped. The result is that the detector only does heavy computation on points that have actually changed, trading a small amount of accuracy for a large speedup. The level of filtering can be tuned to hit different latency vs. accuracy tradeoffs.
